newsitem.title: USA: Diplomats could be prosecuted in New York case.
newsitem.headline: Diplomats could be prosecuted in New York case.

text.p: An investigation of a recent clash between diplomats from Russia and Belarus and New York City police found sufficient evidence for prosecution, the Manhattan District Attorney's office said on Wednesday.

"Based on our investigation, we have concluded that the police officers acted reasonably and appropriately and that the evidence would support criminal charges including driving while intoxicated, resisting arrest, harassment and disorderly conduct," Robert Morgenthau, the district attorney said.
Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who said that the two men had clearly abused their diplomatic privileges and demanded they be either prosecuted or expelled from the United States, welcomed the finding.
"From day one, I have asked the State Department to support us in our efforts to have both of these diplomats prosecuted ... or expelled," Giuliani told a news conference.
The State Department must now decide if it will lift immunity on the officials so they can be prosecuted.
The diplomats, First Secretary Boris Obnossov of Russia and Yuri Orange of Belarus, have given conflicting accounts since the Dec. 29, 1996, incident in Manhattan.
The prosecutor said two officers pulled Obnossov from a car because he appeared intoxicated after parking illegally near a fire hydrant. Investigators said Orange then punched one of the officers.

"The police officers' observations of Mr. Obnossov's intoxicated condition are corroborated by civilian eyewitnesses and other independent evidence," Morgenthau said in a letter to the State Department on Wednesday.
But Dmitri Seoktistov, deputy press secretary at the Russian Federation Mission to the United Nations, said "The District Attorney has sided with one party in this dispute exclusively."
"The accusations are not proof of guilt and we do not consider ourselves committed to the results of the investigation by the district attorney," he added.
Obnossov told a December news conference that when he produced his diplomatic identification, "the officer threw it on the floor of my car.
"I never resisted any law enforcement action. Even in this case, I did not resist at all," he said. He accused one of the officers of being "rude, aggressive and nervously unstable."

The mayor accused the State Department "of backing off with decisive action" in the case. "The slightest bit of annoyance expressed by the U.N. and our State Department runs and hides. I hope that the State Department now acts."
